content:
OpenAI filed counterclaims against Apple in a California federal court on Friday, accusing the iPhone maker of stealing its trade secrets and pressuring hardware suppliers to block its entry into the market for artificial intelligence devices. The filing, reported first by the Financial Times, turns the tables in a legal fight that Apple started in July, and it sets up a courtroom battle over who will control the next generation of personal gadgets.

The ChatGPT maker accused Apple of "unlawful, tortious, and unfair business practices" in its Friday filing in the Northern District of California. According to [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/technology/openai-countersues-apple-stealing-trade-secrets-ft-reports-2026-11-27/), OpenAI says Apple gained confidential information by re-hiring a former employee who had spent six months at OpenAI, where he gained access to specific information on a new device as well as the company's roadmap for future hardware products.

"Given the timing, it now appears that stealing those documents may have been his reason for joining OpenAI in the first place," OpenAI said in the filing, according to Reuters. The countersuit alleges that the employee sent dozens of OpenAI documents about a prototype to his personal phone numbers, left the company in June, returned to Apple, and then presented OpenAI's plans to senior Apple staff in July, at Apple's request.

Apple denied the allegations. A company spokesperson said in a statement that "this case is about OpenAI employees deliberately stealing, accessing, and using Apple's secret and confidential information regarding our unreleased technologies, processes, and products — not about inadvertent retention of Apple information." The spokesperson called OpenAI's counterclaims "a transparent attempt to distract from the substance of Apple's lawsuit, in which OpenAI has already been ordered to stop using Apple's confidential information."

The dispute began in July, when Apple sued OpenAI and two former Apple employees, Tang Tan and Chang Liu, alleging that they misappropriated Apple's trade secrets to benefit the ChatGPT owner's move into consumer hardware. OpenAI has denied those allegations. In October, OpenAI pledged not to use the information Apple claims as trade secrets, after the judge in the case said he was "highly likely" to issue an order barring OpenAI from using it until trial. On Friday, OpenAI also withdrew its motion to dismiss Apple's case, without giving a reason.

Beyond the employee at the centre of the new filing, OpenAI's counterclaims take aim at how Apple manages its workforce. The filing says Apple encourages employees to do work on their personal Apple devices and accounts, and then prevents them from making an orderly separation of work and personal accounts when they leave for a new job. OpenAI said Apple continues to access former employees' personal devices and accounts after they depart, enabling it to "monitor and ensnare" them when they leave for competitors. The complaint describes these practices as "trapdoors" that let Apple accuse former employees of trade secret theft.

OpenAI said in the filing that 400 employees have left Apple for OpenAI so far, and that Apple wants to intimidate others from leaving to join rival technology companies. The countersuit also accuses Apple of using its size and wealth to stifle competition by threatening suppliers that might work on OpenAI's devices. According to the filing, Apple has demanded that suppliers identify their projects for OpenAI and the employees assigned to them, a pressure campaign OpenAI says is designed to hamper its entry into the connected-devices market.

The stakes go well beyond a pair of lawsuits. The two companies were partners as recently as 2024, when ChatGPT was integrated into Apple products, but they are now poised to become direct rivals. OpenAI is developing its first AI-enabled personal devices with io, the hardware studio led by Apple's renowned former design chief Jony Ive, which OpenAI acquired earlier this year. The complaint argues that those devices threaten to "outcompete Apple on what Apple views as its own turf," and accuses Apple of struggling to incorporate innovative AI capabilities into its previously popular products.

The litigation sets up a contest over devices that may not use traditional apps or operating systems at all — products which, if successful, would direct consumer attention away from Apple's best-selling iPhone. Analysts believe OpenAI is working on a phone or another device of its own, and the hardware race has already reshaped the industry's talent market, with engineers moving between the two companies in both directions.

Both companies have requested a jury trial. The case is the latest front in a wider struggle over AI talent and technology: OpenAI has faced scrutiny from regulators and lawmakers over its own practices, including a congressional probe into a reported deal that would let ByteDance use OpenAI models through Microsoft's Azure cloud, as covered in [Global Wire's earlier report](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/microsoft-bytedance-openai-azure-deal-house-probe-november-2026). Apple, meanwhile, has had its own difficult year, including a [major outage of its cloud services](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/apple-services-outage-icloud-app-store-apple-pay-november-2026) earlier this month.

Neither company commented beyond the court filings and Apple's statement on Friday. With the countersuit filed, the two sides now accuse each other of the same offence — stealing trade secrets to win the race for the device that comes after the smartphone — and it will be a jury in San Jose that decides which version of events to believe.
summary: OpenAI countersued Apple on Friday, accusing the iPhone maker of stealing its trade secrets and pressuring suppliers, in a legal fight over who will build the next generation of AI-powered personal devices.
title: OpenAI countersues Apple, accusing it of stealing trade secrets and pressuring suppliers
